analysis.one_liner: Restricts debt collectors' harassment tactics, bans medical debt from credit reports, and cancels private student loans at death or disability.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee 16 days after introduction, without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tighten rules across nearly every corner of debt collection. It would ban debt collectors from threatening service members with demotion or security-clearance loss, cancel private student loans when a borrower dies or becomes permanently disabled, block medical debts from appearing on credit reports for at least a year and from collections for two years, cap fees charged by collectors working for federal agencies at 10% of what they collect, ban confession-of-judgment clauses in small business and merchant cash advance lending, and raise the penalties collectors can owe for breaking the law. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and received no further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who owe debts: service members and their families, student loan borrowers and their cosigners, patients with medical bills, small business owners facing merchant cash advance lenders, and consumers facing aggressive or repeated electronic collection contacts. Cosigners of private student loans benefit directly because their liability must be discharged alongside the borrower's.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Debtors, service members, patients, students, small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Bans debt collectors from threatening a service member with rank reduction, security clearance revocation, or military prosecution, and orders a government study on collection practices targeting service members [S2].
Requires private education loan holders to discharge a loan when the borrower dies or becomes totally and permanently disabled, and to release any cosigner from liability [S2].

Bars collecting a medical debt in the first two years after the first payment is due, and stops credit bureaus from reporting medical debts from medically necessary procedures at all or other medical debts for at least 365 days [S2].

Caps fees charged by collectors hired by federal or state agencies at 10 percent of the amount collected, requires three advance notices before a federal agency transfers a debt to a private collector, and forbids the Treasury from using private collectors on FEMA disaster-assistance overpayments except in cases of fraud [S2].

Prohibits confessions of judgment and similar waivers of the right to notice and a hearing in small business and merchant cash advance lending, and limits collectors' ability to barrage consumers with emails, texts, and social media messages without consent [S2].

Raises penalties for lawbreaking collectors, including increasing the cap tied to collector revenue from 1 percent of net worth to 5 percent of gross annual revenue, allows courts to grant injunctive relief, and indexes statutory damages to inflation [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Debt collection agencies would lose tactics and revenue; consumer reporting agencies would have less data to sell; private student loan holders would absorb losses on discharged loans; merchant cash advance and small business lenders would lose confession-of-judgment enforcement; federal contractors collecting government debts would face a fee cap.
analysis.who_pays_short: Debt collectors, credit bureaus, private lenders

drawbacks.text: A two-year ban on collecting medical debts could leave health care providers uncompensated longer, which may push hospitals to raise prices for other patients or require upfront payment [S2].

Barring medically necessary procedure debts from credit reports forever removes information lenders have used to price loans, which could make some credit harder to get or more expensive for all borrowers [S2].

Raising the damages cap to 5 percent of a collector's gross annual revenue and allowing injunctions would substantially increase litigation exposure for collection firms, a cost that could consolidate the industry or raise its fees [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target practices that fall hardest on people with little money: service members, disabled borrowers, cosigners, and patients. The main costs are practical, not fiscal: lenders and collectors would bear losses, some credit information would disappear from reports, and medical providers would wait longer for payment. Those tradeoffs are real, but the bill was never examined or debated by either chamber, so no committee weighed them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House in mid-December 2024, referred to the Financial Services Committee, and the Congress ended two weeks later with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Maxine Waters, the ranking Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, introduced the bill on December 18, 2024 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, where it received no further action [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills that have not passed die when a Congress ends [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collection firms, credit reporting agencies, private student loan holders, and merchant cash advance lenders keep the current rules, which the bill would have tightened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Debt collectors and lenders keep the status quo

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.role: U.S. Representative (CA-43), Ranking Member, House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it; as ranking committee member she could not advance it further before the Congress ended.

against.name: Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule a hearing or markup on the bill during the 16 days it sat on the committee's docket.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan split can be measured; the sponsor was a Democrat and the Republican-led committee never acted.

industries.note: The bill bans several of their tactics (military threats, unlimited electronic contact, government-debt fees above 10%), raises penalties to 5 percent of gross annual revenue, and closes some exemptions. Collections would also become harder: no medical debt collection for two years.
The bill blocks reporting of medical debts from medically necessary procedures entirely and other medical debts for at least a year, removing a category of data bureaus sell to lenders.

industries.industry: Private student loan lenders and holders
industries.note: They would have to discharge loans at death or total permanent disability and release cosigners, absorbing losses on loans they currently can pursue for life.

industries.industry: Merchant cash advance and small business lenders
industries.note: A new ban on confession-of-judgment clauses removes their main tool for seizing a borrower's accounts without a hearing.

Fees would be capped at 10 percent of amounts collected and federal agencies would need three notices before referring a debt, cutting their margins and volume, though the bill's expanded definition would newly bring some of them under federal consumer law.
They would lose credit reporting and early collection as tools to get patients to pay, stretching out payment timelines, while patients get breathing room on medical bills.
